questions.question: Which data structure in Python stores data in key-value pairs?
options: List
Tuple
Dictionary
Set
questions.explanation: A dict maps unique, hashable keys to values (e.g. {'name': 'Asha'}); lists and tuples are sequences indexed by position, and a set stores unique values with no associated value.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of NumPy in machine learning?
options: Building web APIs for models
Fast numerical and array operations
Managing relational databases
Plotting interactive dashboards and charts
questions.explanation: NumPy provides the n-dimensional array and vectorized math (broadcasting, linear algebra) that Pandas, scikit-learn and PyTorch build on; plotting and web APIs are handled by other libraries.

questions.question: Which Pandas function is commonly used to read a CSV file?
options: pd.load()
pd.read_csv()
pd.csv()
pd.import()
questions.explanation: pd.read_csv() parses a CSV file into a DataFrame; pd.load() and pd.csv() do not exist, and import is a reserved Python keyword.

questions.question: Which of the following is a supervised learning algorithm?
options: K-Means
Linear Regression
PCA
Apriori
questions.explanation: Linear regression learns from labelled examples (inputs with known target values); K-Means and PCA are unsupervised, and Apriori mines association rules from unlabelled transactions.

questions.question: Which algorithm can be used to predict whether an email is spam or not spam?
options: Linear Regression
Logistic Regression
K-Means
PCA
questions.explanation: Spam detection is binary classification, and logistic regression outputs the probability of the positive class; linear regression predicts unbounded numbers, and K-Means and PCA are unsupervised.

questions.question: Why do we divide a dataset into training and testing data?
options: To make the dataset larger so the model trains for longer
To measure performance on data the model has not seen
To remove all missing values
To reduce the number of features
questions.explanation: The held-out test set stands in for new, unseen data, so the score on it estimates real-world performance; scoring on the training data would reward memorisation.

questions.question: A model performs extremely well on training data but poorly on testing data. What is the most likely problem?
options: Underfitting
Overfitting
Too much regularization
Too few training epochs
questions.explanation: The model has memorised noise specific to the training set and fails to generalise; underfitting, heavy regularization or too few epochs would also give poor training performance.

questions.question: A k-NN classifier uses two unscaled features: age (18 to 70 years) and annual income (200,000 to 5,000,000 rupees). What is the most likely problem, and the fix?
options: Income dominates the distances; standardize both features first
Age dominates the distances; drop the income column to balance it
Nothing; k-NN is unaffected by the units of its features
k-NN needs categories; one-hot encode both features first
questions.explanation: k-NN compares Euclidean distances, so a feature measured in millions swamps one measured in years; standardization ((x - mean) / std, giving mean 0 and std 1) puts both on a comparable scale. Scale-invariant models such as decision trees would not need this.

questions.question: For an imbalanced classification problem, which metric can be more informative than simple accuracy?
options: Precision, recall or F1-score
R² score
Mean squared error
Overall accuracy on the training set
questions.explanation: With 99% negatives, always predicting 'negative' scores 99% accuracy but catches no positives; precision, recall and F1 measure performance on the minority class. R² and MSE are regression metrics.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of an activation function in a neural network?
options: Normalize the input features
Introduce non-linearity
Initialize the weights
Reduce the number of parameters
questions.explanation: Without non-linear activations such as ReLU, a stack of linear layers collapses into one linear transformation, so the network could only learn linear relationships.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of gradient descent?
options: Shuffle the training data
Minimize the model's loss function
Normalize the input features before training
Split the data into batches
questions.explanation: Gradient descent repeatedly moves the parameters a small step opposite to the gradient of the loss, driving them towards a minimum of the loss function; batching is just how the gradient is estimated.

questions.question: Convolutional Neural Networks are particularly useful for which type of problem?
options: Image recognition
Small tabular datasets
Association rule mining
Sorting large arrays
questions.explanation: Convolutions slide small learned filters over the image, capturing local spatial patterns such as edges and textures with shared weights; on small tabular data, tree ensembles usually work better.

questions.question: Which technique converts text into numerical vectors that can be processed by machine-learning models?
options: Tokenization and embeddings
Stemming
Stop-word removal
Part-of-speech (POS) tagging
questions.explanation: Tokenization splits text into tokens mapped to ids, and embeddings (or TF-IDF) turn them into numeric vectors; stemming, stop-word removal and POS tagging still output text or tags.

questions.question: A trained ML model needs to be made available through an application so users can send input and receive predictions. What is commonly used?
options: A REST API (e.g. FastAPI) that wraps the model
A Jupyter notebook shared by email
A CSV file of past predictions
A training script that someone reruns for each user request
questions.explanation: Wrapping the model in a web API, such as a FastAPI /predict endpoint, lets any app send inputs over HTTP and get predictions back; notebooks and manual scripts cannot serve live requests.

questions.question: A fraud model outputs a probability for each transaction, and missing a fraud costs about 50 times more than a false alarm. At the default 0.5 threshold, recall on fraud is only 40%. Without retraining, what is the most sensible change?
options: Lower the threshold, trading more false alarms for higher recall
Raise the threshold to 0.9 so only very confident cases are flagged
Keep 0.5 and switch the reported metric to overall accuracy
Pick the threshold that gives the highest accuracy on the test set
questions.explanation: With a 50:1 cost ratio it pays to flag a transaction even at a low fraud probability (about 1/51, roughly 2%, if the model is calibrated), so lowering the threshold raises recall at the cost of precision; tune it on validation data, not the test set. Maximising accuracy on such imbalanced data pushes the threshold the wrong way, towards flagging almost nothing.

questions.question: Which Python library is widely used for classical machine-learning algorithms such as decision trees and logistic regression?
options: Flask
BeautifulSoup
Pygame
scikit-learn
questions.explanation: scikit-learn implements classical algorithms (decision trees, logistic regression, SVMs, k-means) behind a consistent fit/predict API; Flask is a web framework, BeautifulSoup parses HTML and Pygame builds games.

questions.question: Which technique commonly converts a nominal categorical feature into separate binary indicator columns?
options: One-hot encoding
Label encoding
Standardization
Binning
questions.explanation: One-hot encoding creates one 0/1 column per category (pd.get_dummies or OneHotEncoder); label encoding maps categories to a single integer column, which implies an order nominal data does not have.

questions.question: Which metric measures the average absolute difference between predicted and actual numerical values?
options: Accuracy
Mean Absolute Error (MAE)
Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE)
Log loss
questions.explanation: MAE = mean(|y - ŷ|), the average error in the target's own units; RMSE squares the errors before averaging, so it penalises large errors more heavily.

questions.question: For a numerical feature with strong outliers, which simple imputation value is often more robust than the mean?
options: Maximum
Zero
Median
Standard deviation
questions.explanation: The median is the middle value, so a few extreme outliers barely move it, while they drag the mean towards them; filling with zero or the maximum distorts the distribution.

questions.question: In supervised learning, what is a feature?
options: The final trained model file
An input variable used to make a prediction
The error produced after deployment
A test-set label that stays hidden from the model during training
questions.explanation: Features (X) are the input columns, such as age or income; the target or label (y) is the value the model learns to predict.

questions.question: What is the main idea of k-fold cross-validation?
options: Split into k folds; each fold is the validation set once while the rest train
Train k models on the full dataset and keep the one with the best training score
Split into k folds and train only on the largest fold
Repeat a random split k times, tuning on the test set each time
questions.explanation: Each of the k folds serves once as the validation set while the model trains on the other k-1 folds, and the k scores are averaged, giving a more reliable estimate than a single split.

questions.question: What is the typical effect of L2 regularization in a model?
options: It increases model complexity to reduce bias
It drives many coefficients to exactly zero, performing feature selection
It penalizes large weights, shrinking them to reduce overfitting
It removes correlated features before training
questions.explanation: L2 (ridge) adds λ·Σw² to the loss, shrinking weights smoothly towards zero but rarely to exactly zero; setting coefficients exactly to zero (sparse feature selection) is characteristic of L1/lasso.

questions.question: Which formula represents recall for the positive class?
options: TN / (TN + FP)
TP / (TP + FP)
(TP + TN) / Total
TP / (TP + FN)
questions.explanation: Recall (sensitivity) = TP / (TP + FN), the share of actual positives the model catches; TP / (TP + FP) is precision and TN / (TN + FP) is specificity.

questions.question: What is Principal Component Analysis (PCA) primarily used for?
options: Selecting the original features that are most correlated with the target
Projecting data onto fewer directions that capture the most variance
Clustering similar data points into k groups
Scaling every feature into the range [0, 1]
questions.explanation: PCA finds orthogonal directions of maximum variance and projects the data onto the top few, reducing dimensionality; it ignores the target and builds new combined features rather than selecting original ones.

questions.question: How can class weights help with an imbalanced classification dataset?
options: They make mistakes on the minority class cost more in the loss
They delete majority-class rows until the classes are balanced
They generate synthetic minority samples, like SMOTE
They guarantee equal precision and recall for every class
questions.explanation: class_weight (e.g. 'balanced' in scikit-learn) scales each sample's loss by its class weight, so errors on rare classes are penalised more without changing the data; undersampling and SMOTE modify the dataset instead.

questions.question: Which situation is an example of data leakage?
options: Evaluating the final model exactly once on a separate, held-out test set
Removing exact duplicate rows before splitting the data
Fitting a scaler on the full dataset before the train/test split
Training the same model for a few more epochs
questions.explanation: A scaler (or imputer/encoder) fitted on all rows lets test-set statistics such as the mean and std influence training, making scores optimistic; fit preprocessing on the training split only, ideally inside a scikit-learn Pipeline.

questions.question: What is the main role of the attention mechanism in a Transformer?
options: Process tokens strictly one at a time, like an RNN
Let each token weigh the relevance of all other tokens in its context
Remove stop words and punctuation before the text ever reaches the model
Map each word to a fixed one-hot vector
questions.explanation: Self-attention builds each token's representation as a weighted sum over all tokens, with weights from query-key similarity, so meaning depends on context; it also lets Transformers process tokens in parallel instead of one by one.

questions.question: A model has high error on both the training set and validation set. Which issue is most likely?
options: Data leakage
High variance / overfitting
A validation set that is too small
High bias / underfitting
questions.explanation: If the model cannot even fit the training data, it is too simple or over-regularized (high bias); high variance would show low training error but much higher validation error.

questions.question: What does concept drift mean in a deployed machine-learning system?
options: The relationship between the inputs and the target changes over time
Only the input feature distribution shifts, while P(y | x) stays the same
The model's weights slowly change by themselves after deployment
Prediction latency gradually increases as traffic grows
questions.explanation: Concept drift means P(y | x) changes, e.g. fraud patterns evolve, so the same inputs now map to different outcomes; a shift in the inputs alone with P(y | x) unchanged is data (covariate) drift.

questions.question: A binary classifier is well calibrated. What should a predicted probability of about 0.8 mean over many similar cases?
options: The model is correct on every such case
The positive class appears exactly 80 times in every batch of 100 cases
About 80% of such cases turn out positive in the long run
The decision threshold should be set to 0.8
questions.explanation: Calibration is a long-run frequency property: among many predictions near 0.8, about 80% should be positive. It does not promise exact counts in any single batch or dictate the decision threshold.

questions.question:
What does this code print?

nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
print([n * n for n in nums if n % 2 == 1])
questions.explanation: The condition n % 2 == 1 keeps only the odd numbers 1, 3 and 5, and the expression n * n squares them, giving [1, 9, 25].

questions.question: Which Git command saves your staged changes as a new snapshot in the local repository's history?
options: git push
git add
git clone
git commit
questions.explanation: git commit records the staged changes as a new commit in the local repository; git add only stages changes, and git push uploads existing commits to a remote such as GitHub.

questions.question: Which of these can be used as a key in a Python dictionary?
options: A list such as [1, 2]
A set such as {1, 2}
A dict such as {'a': 1}
A tuple such as (1, 2)
questions.explanation: Dictionary keys must be hashable: an immutable tuple of hashable items is, whereas lists, sets and dicts are mutable and raise TypeError: unhashable type.

questions.question: In NumPy, a has shape (3, 1) and b has shape (1, 4). What is the shape of a + b?
options: It raises a ValueError
questions.explanation: Broadcasting stretches size-1 dimensions to match: (3, 1) and (1, 4) are compatible in every dimension, so the result has shape (3, 4).

questions.question:
What does this code print?

class Model:
    count = 0
    def __init__(self):
        Model.count += 1

a = Model()
b = Model()
print(Model.count, a.count)
options: AttributeError
questions.explanation: count is a class attribute shared by all instances; each __init__ increments Model.count, so it becomes 2, and a.count finds no instance attribute and falls back to the same class attribute.

questions.question: Your Jupyter notebook worked all day, but after 'Restart Kernel and Run All' it fails with a NameError. What is the most likely cause?
options: Restarting the kernel uninstalls the packages you imported
Run All executes the cells from the bottom up
The restart silently switched the notebook to an older Python interpreter
It used a variable from a cell you later edited or deleted (hidden state)
questions.explanation: The kernel remembers every variable from every cell you ran, in any order, so a clean top-to-bottom run exposes code that depends on cells you changed or removed; a restart clears memory, not installed packages.

questions.question:
What does this code print?

import numpy as np
a = np.arange(5)
b = a[1:4]
b[0] = 99
print(a.tolist())
questions.explanation: Basic slicing of a NumPy array returns a view that shares memory with the original, so b[0] is a[1]; use a[1:4].copy() for an independent array (plain Python list slices, by contrast, copy).

questions.question:
What does this code print?

def add_item(item, bucket=[]):
    bucket.append(item)
    return bucket

add_item(1)
print(add_item(2))
options: TypeError
questions.explanation: A default value is evaluated once, when the function is defined, so every call that omits bucket shares the same list; the idiomatic fix is bucket=None and creating a new list inside.

questions.question: You must count the error lines in a 20 GB log file using Python on a laptop with 8 GB of RAM. Which approach works?
options: Call f.readlines() and loop over the returned list
Read everything with f.read().splitlines(), then count the matching lines
Load it with a single pd.read_csv() call, then filter
Loop over the open file object (for line in f), one line at a time
questions.explanation: A file object is a lazy iterator that yields one line at a time, so memory use stays tiny; readlines(), read() and a single read_csv() call all try to load the whole 20 GB into RAM.

questions.question: Which SQL clause filters individual rows before any grouping is done?
options: HAVING
ORDER BY
WHERE
GROUP BY
questions.explanation: WHERE filters rows before GROUP BY forms groups; HAVING filters the groups afterwards, which is why it can use aggregates such as COUNT(*).

questions.question:
Given

df = pd.DataFrame({'city': ['Pune', 'Delhi', 'Pune', 'Delhi'],
                   'sales': [10, 20, 30, 40]})

what is df.groupby('city')['sales'].mean()['Delhi']?
questions.explanation: groupby('city') splits the rows by city; Delhi's sales are 20 and 40, so their mean is 30.0 (60 would be the sum and 25.0 the overall mean).

questions.question: During EDA, a histogram of household income shows a long tail to the right. How do the mean and median typically compare?
options: The mean is greater than the median
The median is greater than the mean
They are equal, as in any distribution
It depends only on the sample size
questions.explanation: A few very large incomes in the right tail pull the mean upwards while the median (the middle value) barely moves, so mean > median; this is why median income is usually reported.

questions.question: Matrix A has shape (4, 3) and matrix B has shape (3, 2). What is the shape of the product A @ B?
options: The product is undefined
questions.explanation: Matrix multiplication needs matching inner dimensions (3 and 3) and returns the outer ones, so (4, 3) @ (3, 2) gives (4, 2); a dense neural-network layer applies exactly this to a batch of inputs.

questions.question: A disease affects 1% of people. A test detects it 90% of the time when it is present, and gives a false positive 10% of the time when it is absent. If a random person tests positive, roughly what is the probability that they have the disease?
options: About 90%
About 50%
About 1%
About 8%
questions.explanation: P(disease | +) = (0.9 × 0.01) / (0.9 × 0.01 + 0.1 × 0.99) = 0.009 / 0.108 ≈ 8%: false positives from the 99% healthy majority outnumber the true positives (the base-rate fallacy).

questions.question:
students has 100 rows (one per student). You run

pd.merge(students, marks, on='student_id', how='left')

and the result has 250 rows. What is the most likely reason?
options: how='left' keeps every row from both DataFrames
Many students have several matching rows in marks (one per subject)
Students with no marks are duplicated to fill the NaNs
merge() silently falls back to a cross join whenever the key column repeats
questions.explanation: A merge emits one row per matching key pair, so a one-to-many relationship multiplies student rows; how='left' keeps unmatched students once (with NaN marks) and never adds unmatched rows from marks, which is what how='outer' does.

questions.question: Which query lists every employee with the rank of their salary within their own department, without collapsing rows?
options: SELECT name, dept, salary, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) FROM emp ORDER BY dept;
SELECT dept, MAX(salary) FROM emp GROUP BY dept;
SELECT name, dept, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) FROM emp;
SELECT name, dept, salary FROM emp ORDER BY dept, salary DESC;
questions.explanation: PARTITION BY dept restarts the ranking for each department while keeping every row; GROUP BY collapses rows to one per group, and OVER without PARTITION BY ranks across the whole table.

questions.question: Your dataset has several chest X-ray images per patient. Random 5-fold cross-validation gives 97% accuracy, but accuracy on new patients is only 70%. What is the most likely flaw and fix?
options: Five folds are too few; use 10-fold CV so each validation fold is more reliable
The model is underfitting; add more layers and train for more epochs
The classes are imbalanced; use StratifiedKFold so each fold keeps the same class ratios
Same-patient images leak across folds; use GroupKFold with patient ID as the group
questions.explanation: Images of one patient are highly correlated, so random folds let the model recognise patients it has already seen; GroupKFold keeps each patient in a single fold, mimicking truly new patients. Stratification fixes class ratios, not this leakage.

questions.question: In neural-network training, what is one epoch?
options: One full pass over the entire training dataset
One weight update computed from a single mini-batch of samples
The number of layers in the network
The time taken to process one sample
questions.explanation: An epoch is one complete pass over all training samples; with 10,000 samples and a batch size of 100, one epoch contains 100 iterations (weight updates).

questions.question: In a standard PyTorch training loop, why is optimizer.zero_grad() called before loss.backward() on every iteration?
options: It resets the model's weights to zero before each update
It sets the learning rate to zero during warm-up
Gradients accumulate in .grad by default, so old ones must be cleared
It frees the GPU memory held by the computation graph from the last batch
questions.explanation: loss.backward() adds new gradients to whatever is already stored in each parameter's .grad, so without zero_grad() gradients from earlier batches pile up and corrupt the update; the weights are untouched.

questions.question: Training loss keeps falling, but validation loss has been rising since epoch 8. Which technique directly addresses this?
options: Increase the model size so it can learn more
Raise the learning rate to escape the plateau
Remove the dropout layers so the network can fit the data more closely
Early stopping: keep the checkpoint with the best validation loss
questions.explanation: Rising validation loss with falling training loss means the network has started to overfit; early stopping halts training (or restores the best checkpoint) at the epoch with the lowest validation loss.

questions.question: A 32×32 RGB image passes through a Conv2d layer with 16 filters, kernel size 3, stride 1 and no padding. What is the output shape (channels × height × width)?
questions.explanation: Output size = (W - K + 2P) / S + 1 = (32 - 3 + 0) / 1 + 1 = 30, and each of the 16 filters produces one channel; padding=1 would keep the size at 32 × 32.

questions.question: While training a neural network, the loss jumps around wildly and soon becomes NaN. What should you try first?
options: Increase the learning rate
Train for more epochs
Lower the learning rate
Add more hidden layers
questions.explanation: A learning rate that is too large makes updates overshoot the minimum, so the loss oscillates and can explode to NaN; lowering it (optionally with gradient clipping) is the standard first fix.

questions.question: Why do LSTMs handle long sequences better than vanilla RNNs?
options: They process the entire sequence in parallel using self-attention instead
They use ReLU everywhere, so gradients can never vanish
They have no recurrent connections to backpropagate through
Their gated cell state lets gradients flow across many time steps
questions.explanation: In a vanilla RNN the gradient is multiplied by the recurrent weights at every step and shrinks exponentially; the LSTM's additive cell-state path, controlled by forget/input/output gates, keeps the signal alive. Parallel self-attention is the Transformer's idea, not the LSTM's.

questions.question: You have only 2,000 labelled images of crop diseases. Which approach is most likely to give the best accuracy quickly?
options: Fine-tune an ImageNet-pretrained CNN, with its early layers frozen at first
Train a deep CNN from scratch with random weights for 500 epochs
Flatten the pixels and train a logistic regression model
Train a large Vision Transformer from scratch on just the 2,000 labelled images
questions.explanation: A pretrained network already knows generic visual features (edges, textures, shapes), so fine-tuning it on a small dataset converges fast and overfits less; deep models trained from scratch on 2,000 images overfit badly.

questions.question: Your PyTorch model gives different predictions for the same input on every call, and accuracy is below what you saw in validation. The inference code never calls model.eval(). Which layers are most likely responsible?
options: Linear and Conv2d, whose weights keep updating at inference
The loss function and optimizer, which still run on each call
Dropout and BatchNorm, which behave differently in training mode
Embedding layers, which re-randomise their vectors every time they are called
questions.explanation: In training mode dropout randomly zeroes activations and BatchNorm uses the current batch's statistics; model.eval() disables dropout and switches BatchNorm to its running averages, making inference deterministic. Weights only change when optimizer.step() runs.

questions.question: A one-weight model computes y = w · x with loss L = (y - 10)². For x = 3 and w = 2, what is the gradient dL/dw?
questions.explanation: y = 6, so dL/dy = 2(y - 10) = -8 and dy/dw = x = 3; by the chain rule dL/dw = -8 × 3 = -24 (the negative sign means increasing w lowers the loss).

questions.question: Why is a model's prediction API usually packaged in a Docker container before deployment?
options: It makes the model's predictions more accurate
It runs with the same Python version and dependencies everywhere
It compresses the model weights so that inference needs almost no RAM
It removes the need for a framework like FastAPI
questions.explanation: A Docker image bundles the code, Python version, libraries and system packages, so the service behaves the same on a laptop, in CI and in the cloud; it does not change the model's accuracy.

questions.question: In a semantic search system, which measure is most commonly used to compare two text embedding vectors?
options: Edit (Levenshtein) distance
Exact string match
Cosine similarity
Difference in word counts
questions.explanation: Cosine similarity measures the angle between two embedding vectors, so texts with similar meaning score close to 1 even without shared words; edit distance and exact matching compare raw characters.

questions.question: What is a key architectural difference between BERT and GPT-style models?
options: BERT: decoder that generates text left to right; GPT: bidirectional encoder trained on masked tokens
BERT is built on RNNs, while GPT is built on Transformers
BERT works only on images, while GPT works only on text
BERT: encoder trained on masked tokens; GPT: decoder trained on next-token prediction
questions.explanation: BERT uses a bidirectional Transformer encoder pretrained by predicting masked tokens, which suits classification and embeddings; GPT uses a causal decoder trained to predict the next token, which suits generation. Both are Transformers.

questions.question: In a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) chatbot over company PDFs, what happens when a user asks a question?
options: Relevant chunks are retrieved from a vector index and added to the LLM's prompt
The LLM is fine-tuned on the PDFs again for every new question
The PDFs are converted to SQL tables and queried with SQL
The LLM answers only from its pre-training data, and the PDFs are just logged for audits
questions.explanation: RAG embeds the question, retrieves the most similar document chunks from a vector store and passes them to the LLM as context, grounding answers in current documents without retraining; fine-tuning per query would be slow and costly.

questions.question: What is MLflow Tracking mainly used for in an ML project?
options: Labelling raw images and text for supervised learning
Load-balancing prediction traffic across Kubernetes pods
Logging parameters, metrics and artifacts for each training run
Automatically searching for the best neural-network architecture for a task
questions.explanation: MLflow Tracking records each run's hyperparameters, metrics and artifacts (models, plots) in one place, so experiments can be compared and the best model reproduced or registered.

questions.question: A loan-approval model was trained on 2023 data. Applicant incomes have since shifted, and true repayment labels arrive only after 6 months. What is the best way to detect problems early?
options: Wait until the repayment labels arrive, and only then compare accuracy with the 2023 baseline
Retrain daily, treating the model's own predictions as the new ground-truth labels
Track only API latency and HTTP error rates, since they reflect model quality
Compare live input distributions with training data (e.g. PSI, KS test) and alert on drift
questions.explanation: When labels are delayed, input (data) drift is the earliest signal: PSI or a Kolmogorov-Smirnov test flags live features that no longer resemble the training data. Training on the model's own predictions reinforces its errors, and latency says nothing about accuracy.

questions.question: Your FastAPI service loads a 1 GB model from disk inside the /predict endpoint function, and every request takes about 4 seconds. What is the best fix?
options: Load the model once at application startup and reuse it across requests
Add more Uvicorn workers so that each one can reload the model in parallel
Raise the request timeout so that slow responses don't fail
Return a placeholder prediction while the model is still loading
questions.explanation: Loading per request repeats an expensive disk read and deserialisation every time; loading once at startup (e.g. in FastAPI's lifespan handler) keeps the model in memory so each request only runs inference. More workers or longer timeouts only hide the symptom.

questions.question: Roughly what happens to the compute and memory of standard self-attention when the input sequence length doubles?
options: It roughly doubles, since cost grows linearly with the tokens
It stays roughly the same, since all tokens are processed in parallel on a GPU
It grows by a small constant, since only one layer is added
It roughly quadruples, since scores are computed for every pair of tokens
questions.explanation: Standard self-attention builds an n × n score matrix, so its cost grows as O(n²) and doubling n gives about 4×; this is why long contexts are expensive. Parallelism speeds things up but does not reduce the total work.
